title: Dante's Story: The Baby
description: A-level results day, Emma's arrival, and the collapse of Dante's university plans.
content_html:
The Morning Everything Changes

The novel opens on one of the most significant days of Dante Bridgeman's life: the morning of his A-level results. At seventeen, Dante has a clear vision of his future. He wants to study journalism at university — a goal that feels within reach as he waits for the envelope that will confirm his place. His younger brother Adam narrates the opening passages in parallel, and the dual narration is Blackman's central structural device: two brothers, two sets of preoccupations, one household about to be shaken by the same shock.

Dante's results are good. For a brief moment, the future he planned seems confirmed. Then the doorbell rings.

Emma Arrives

At the door is Emma Bryce — Dante's ex-girlfriend, with whom he split up approximately a year earlier. She is not alone. She has arrived with a baby girl in a pushchair. The baby — named Mel — is approximately ten months old. She cannot yet walk, but she is alert, responsive, and old enough to have a developing personality. Dante is stunned.

Emma tells Dante that Mel is his daughter. The timeline adds up: their relationship ended while Emma was pregnant, though she has kept this from him entirely. Dante had no knowledge of the pregnancy. He has missed the first ten months of his child's life — not through choice, but through deception.

Key Fact

Mel arrives in a pushchair and is approximately ten months old. She is not a newborn. Blackman chose this age deliberately: Mel is old enough to have needs and reactions, but young enough that Dante — who knows nothing about babies — finds her completely overwhelming.

The Deception and the Disappearance

Emma does not announce that she is leaving for good. Her method of abandonment is deceptive, and the deception is what makes it so devastating. She asks Dante to look after Mel while she pops out — the implication is that she will return. She does not return. Later, she sends a text message telling Dante that she will not be coming back.

There is no dramatic confrontation at the door, no tearful goodbye, no conversation about what happens next. Emma exits his life as quietly as possible, leaving Dante with Mel and no instruction, no preparation, and no support beyond his family. The casual brutality of a text message — not even a phone call — encapsulates Emma's refusal to take accountability.

Had Emma been honest about not wanting to return, Dante could have chosen how to respond. Instead she removes his agency. He is left in a situation not of his choosing, with a child he has known for one afternoon, unable to contact the mother, and unsure whether this is permanent. Blackman uses this to underline one of the novel's recurring themes: men can be the primary carers, whether they choose to be or not. Dante's journey into fatherhood begins not with a decision but with a deception.

Dante's First Response

Dante's initial reaction is shock. He does not immediately bond with Mel, nor does he immediately reject her. He is simply at a loss. He does not know how to hold her, how to soothe her, what she needs, or what he is supposed to do. The novel is honest about the learning curve: parenting is not instinctive for Dante. It is learned, slowly and sometimes painfully, over the course of the novel.

His father, Tyler — a widower who raised Dante and Adam alone after losing his wife to cancer — plays a crucial role in the early stages. Tyler's response to Mel is important: he does not condemn Dante. He accepts the situation and helps with the practicalities, modelling the same kind of stoic parental responsibility that has defined his own life. Blackman uses Tyler to show that single fatherhood is not extraordinary — it is what men in this family do.

Key Fact

The boys' mother died of cancer. Tyler has raised Dante and Adam as a widower. This is not an abandonment story — it is a family shaped by grief. Tyler's emotional guardedness stems from unprocessed loss, not bitterness at being left.

University Plans Collapse

Dante had planned to study journalism at university. This ambition is not vague — it is specific and carefully chosen. Within hours of receiving his results, that plan is in ruins. He cannot leave Mel with no one to care for her. He cannot go to university and take a baby. His academic achievement, the thing he has worked towards for two years, becomes meaningless in a single afternoon.

Blackman is deliberate about naming Dante's subject. Journalism is not a trivial aspiration — it is a career built on telling the truth, investigating the world, giving people a voice. The irony is that Dante is now silenced by his circumstances. His story, for the moment, is not one he can tell publicly. He is not the correspondent he wanted to become. He is a teenage father in his dad's house, learning to warm a bottle.

Critics have noted that Dante's career aspiration is meaningful within the novel's structure. Both boys are co-narrators — they tell their own stories in their own voices. In a sense, they are both already journalists of their own experience. Dante's voice is direct, practical, and observational. His frustrated dream becomes part of what he has to rebuild by the novel's end: a sense of a future that includes both Mel and the version of himself he was going to become.

The Dual-Narration Structure

Lesson 2 is also the right moment to consolidate understanding of Blackman's structural choice. The novel alternates between Dante's first-person chapters and Adam's first-person chapters. Each brother sees only his own crisis clearly; neither is fully aware of the other's. Dante is consumed by Mel. Adam is consumed by his own story — his relationship with Josh, his experiences at school, his sense of isolation.

The dual narration creates dramatic irony. We, as readers, see both boys struggling simultaneously. We understand the pressure building in the household before either brother fully articulates it. This technique also makes the novel's climax — when the two storylines violently converge — all the more powerful.
exam_tip_html: For Edexcel, practise linking plot details to themes. When writing about Dante's story, make sure you can connect Emma's method of abandonment (the deception, the text message) to Blackman's theme of male responsibility thrust upon someone without choice. Examiners reward analysis that explains how a specific structural or narrative choice — like dual narration — creates meaning for the reader, not just what happens.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Dante plans to study journalism at university — a specific ambition that Blackman names deliberately.
  • Mel arrives in a pushchair at approximately ten months old; Emma's abandonment is deceptive — she leaves under the pretence of going out and texts later to say she will not return.
  • Tyler is a widower whose wife died of cancer; his steady response to the crisis models single fatherhood as something ordinary in this family, rooted in grief rather than abandonment.
  • The dual-narration structure gives readers simultaneous access to both brothers' crises, generating dramatic irony that builds towards the violent convergence of their storylines.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present Dante's reaction to the arrival of Mel in the opening sections of the novel? You should consider the context in which the novel was written.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of Dante's shock and disorientation. Discusses: his specific career aspiration (journalism), the moment plans collapse, the learning curve of care, Tyler as a model of paternal responsibility. Links to context: changing expectations of fatherhood in early 21st-century Britain, Blackman's interest in male emotional experience. Comments on Blackman's structural choice of dual narration.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant textual support.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Blackman uses Emma Bryce's behaviour to raise questions about responsibility and accountability in the novel.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive discussion of Emma's deceptive method of abandonment. Discusses: the pretence of going out, the text message, the contrast with Dante who stays and takes responsibility. Links to context: parental responsibility in modern Britain, gender and expectation, the novel as a challenge to the assumption that fatherhood is a secondary role. Comments on Blackman's choice to keep Emma largely offstage.
Top band (16-20): Clear argument with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited discussion.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use the dual-narration structure of the novel to create meaning for the reader?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of structural technique. Discusses: alternating first-person chapters, dramatic irony from simultaneous access to both brothers' crises, how the structure builds towards the climactic convergence of storylines, and how each brother's blindness to the other's suffering reflects the novel's theme of hidden pain. Links to Blackman's intentions about male emotional life.
Top band (16-20): Clear structural analysis.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant discussion.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: "Tyler Bridgeman is the novel's most important example of responsible parenthood." How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Convincing argument. Agrees: Tyler models stoic, practical, accepting fatherhood; his response to Mel is steady and supportive; he raised two boys alone as a widower. Complicates: his emotional guardedness also damages Dante and Adam — he cannot express grief or vulnerability. Concludes: Tyler is responsible but emotionally incomplete; Dante must become a fuller version of fatherhood than Tyler.
Top band (16-20): Balanced argument.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some engagement.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Limited discussion.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman present the impact of unexpected parenthood on Dante's sense of identity and future?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive discussion of identity crisis. Discusses: journalism as specific, chosen future now denied; the gap between the self Dante was building and the father he must become; the novel's arc as Dante finding a way to hold both identities. Context: youth aspirations, social mobility, the costs of unplanned parenthood. Blackman's empathetic portrayal of Dante as a victim of circumstance as well as a young man who grows.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Blackman use the opening chapters of the novel to establish the central conflicts that will drive the plot?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25): Perceptive analysis of opening structure. Discusses: dual narration introducing both brothers' crises on the same morning; Dante's results and plans contrasted with their immediate destruction; Adam's storyline introduced in parallel but not yet fully revealed; the household as a pressure-cooker. Blackman's technique of withholding information while creating dramatic tension.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant discussion.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

knowledge_checks.q: What subject does Dante plan to study at university?
How old is Mel when Emma arrives at the Bridgeman house?
options: A few days old — a newborn

knowledge_checks.q: How does Emma tell Dante she is not coming back? (Complete the answer: _____)
options: She tells him face to face at the door

knowledge_checks.q: The boys' mother _____ — she did not leave the family voluntarily.
options: left when the boys were young

knowledge_checks.q: Match each character to their role in Lesson 2:
right: Has his university plans destroyed by the arrival of Mel
Abandons Mel through a deceptive pretence of going out
Models steady, practical fatherhood as a widower

flashcard_questions.q: What is Dante's specific university ambition?
flashcard_questions.a: To study journalism — a career built on investigating and telling the truth.

flashcard_questions.q: How old is Mel when Emma brings her to Dante?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately ten months old — she arrives in a pushchair, not as a newborn.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Emma abandon Mel with Dante?
flashcard_questions.a: She asks Dante to babysit while she goes out, then never returns — later texting to say she will not come back.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to the boys' mother?
flashcard_questions.a: She died of cancer. Tyler has raised Dante and Adam alone as a widower.

flashcard_questions.q: What narrative technique does Blackman use to tell the story?
flashcard_questions.a: Dual first-person narration — Dante and Adam alternate chapters, each telling his own story.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect does the dual narration create for the reader?
flashcard_questions.a: Dramatic irony — we see both brothers' crises simultaneously, even though neither is fully aware of the other's.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Dante's journalism ambition matter thematically?
flashcard_questions.a: Journalism is about truth and voice — Dante's plans are silenced by his circumstances, but the novel charts his recovery of a future.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is Tyler's response to Mel significant?
flashcard_questions.a: He accepts the situation calmly and helps practically, modelling single fatherhood as something this family already knows.

glossary_terms.definition: A wheeled chair for transporting a small child. Mel arrives in a pushchair, signalling she is approximately ten months old — not a newborn.
Being answerable for one's actions and willing to deal directly with their consequences. Emma's text message avoids the accountability of a direct conversation.
A narrative technique in which two characters take turns telling the story in their own first-person voices. Blackman uses this to give Dante and Adam equal weight.
Where the reader knows something a character does not. The dual narration means we see both brothers' crises before they are fully aware of each other's.
A steep and demanding process of acquiring new skills quickly. Dante's parenting journey begins with no preparation and no experience.
